description: I'm Pehlaj, a Senior AI Engineer from Lahore with 4+ years building LLM agents, RAG and production ML. I've shipped AI products end to end and worked on models for Google Gemini, OpenAI and Meta. I'll lead the AI/ML side and get a working prototype up fast. Looking for: a frontend/full-stack dev, a data scientist with satellite or climate data experience, and a designer for the pitch and demo video. Let's build something useful!
summary: AeroPlay is a free, browser-based space game and learning site that lets kids aged 7–12 run a Moon or Mars outpost and feel the real engineering trade-offs that decide whether a mission survives. Every sol, players split a small number of power cells between oxygen, food, radiation shielding, science and the radio to Earth. There is never enough for everything: saving power today can mean going hungry later, and skipping the radio means no storm warning tomorrow. The danger is real. Every solar flare and radiation storm comes from NASA’s DONKI space weather database, each mission day matches a real day on the Sun, and Mars missions use the real Earth–Mars distance to set the radio delay. A live “Mission Control” dashboard shows kids what the Sun, Mars and Earth are doing right now, using NASA DONKI, Curiosity, Perseverance, EPIC, JPL Horizons and OSDR data. AeroPlay turns abstract space facts into decisions kids own, so they leave understanding why astronauts budget every watt, every breath and every dose of radiation.
details:
AeroPlay has two parts:

  1. Outpost Commander (the game). Pick the Moon’s south pole or Mars’s Jezero Crater, pack a lander with only 4 cargo slots, and keep a crew of 4 alive for 20 sols. Each sol you assign power cells to:
    Unused power charges a small battery. Event cards (clogged air filters, sick plants, micrometeorites, ice discoveries) always give two choices, and both cost something. You can shelter the crew when a storm warning arrives, but that stops science, and some warnings are false alarms. On Mars, “Ask Mission Control” shows that a reply takes 2 × 11–22 minutes, so the crew must decide alone.
    • an oxygen maker (the crew breathes 12 units a sol; each cell makes 5),
    • a greenhouse (food arrives 3 sols later, and plants wilt without power),
    • regolith shielding (permanent protection),
    • science, which only counts once the radio sends it home,
    • the radio, which also brings Earth’s storm warnings.
    • this week’s solar flares, eruptions and radiation storms,
    • where NASA’s WSA‑ENLIL model predicts each eruption will hit,
    • the latest NASA forecaster alert, rewritten in kid-friendly words,
    • Curiosity’s latest Mars weather and Perseverance’s newest photo,
    • today’s Earth–Mars distance and radio delay,
    • today’s EPIC photo of Earth,
    • six real NASA OSDR space-biology studies.

How the NASA data drives the game

  • Each mission plays back a real 20-day stretch of DONKI flare and radiation-storm records, either live (the last 20 days) or one of 10 archived storm periods from 2011–2025, such as the September 2017 X9.3 flares and the May 2024 superstorm.
  • Radiation on the Moon is about 2× Mars, matching published measurements: 1.37 mSv/day (Chang’e‑4) vs 0.64 mSv/day (Curiosity RAD).
  • On Mars, the real planet positions decide whether a storm seen from Earth also reaches Mars.
  • Every number is labelled LIVE or ARCHIVE, and the game explains which values are scaled for play.

Benefits and impact
Kids learn engineering trade-offs by making them, not by reading about them. Missions take about 10 minutes, every playthrough is different, and failing isn’t scary: the crew is always rescued, and the debrief shows which choice caused it. The game works in any browser with no account, has a “Read to me” button and a word helper for terms like sol and radiation dose, and suits classrooms (for example, compare the Moon and Mars on the same storm dates).

Tools

  • HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript (no frameworks), with hand-written SVG illustrations
  • Python and curl to download and prepare the NASA data
  • Vercel for hosting and GitHub for the code
  • Claude (Anthropic) as an AI coding and writing assistant
